transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in today?

Well, honestly, I wasn't even sure if I should make this appointment, but... well, I'm just really scared. See, I work as an order filler down at the warehouse, and usually it's pretty loud in there, you know? You've got the forklifts backing up and people yelling across the floor. But the other day, I was in one of the back aisles, completely alone pulling some stock, and I heard my name called out. Just clear as day. I turned around thinking maybe my supervisor needed a pallet moved or something, but there was absolutely nobody in the aisle with me. I walked all the way to the end of the rack, and it was completely empty. 

And then... then it started happening at home, too. I'll just be standing near the hallway, maybe sorting the laundry or just walking to the kitchen, and I hear it again. Just my name being called out from the hall. And the thing that really terrified me—what actually made me finally come in today—is that it doesn't sound like a trick of the ears or an echo or anything like that. It sounds just as real as if my husband were standing right next to me, talking right into my ear. But I turn around, and the hallway is completely empty. My husband isn't even in the room. It's just... it's really messing with my head, you know? Because how can a voice sound so solid and real when there isn't a single soul standing there?
Have you heard any other voices or sounds that others around you don't seem to hear, or has it only been your name being called?

No, it’s... it’s just my name. I haven't heard anything else, thank God. But I tell you, when it happens, I just freeze. Like, I’ll be standing there in the hallway with a pile of towels, and I hear it, and my heart just drops right into my stomach. I stop breathing, and I just listen so hard, thinking, 'Okay, what are they going to say next? Is someone going to start talking to me? Is there a radio on somewhere? Did the neighbors leave their TV blasting?' 

I'll stand there for what feels like ten minutes, just straining my ears, waiting for footsteps or a sentence or a whisper or... or anything. But there’s nothing else. Never a full conversation, never any weird music or ringing or anything like that. Just my name. And then this terrible, heavy silence right after. 

I even asked my husband the other day, I said, 'Did you hear someone talking out on the street? Did you hear a car go by with the radio too loud?' And he just looked at me like I had two heads and said the house was completely quiet. So it's just the one word. Just my name. But honestly, the way it just hangs there in the empty air... it's enough to make you feel like your brain is playing some kind of sick joke on you, you know? I keep waiting for the voice to say something else, but it never, ever does.
Have you seen or felt anything unusual, like seeing someone who wasn't there or feeling something that others don't seem to feel?

No, no, I haven't seen anything. No shadows or people standing in the corner or anything spooky like that. And I haven't felt anything weird either, like, I don't know, things touching me or whatever. I know sometimes people talk about seeing things out of the corner of their eye, but my vision is completely fine. Honestly, if I started seeing people in my house who weren't actually there, I think I'd probably have a heart attack right on the spot and you'd be seeing me in the emergency room instead of here. 

But no, it's really just... well, like I was trying to explain before, it's just the hearing part. That's the whole reason I'm sitting in this chair today. What scared me enough to actually come in and make this appointment is just that I’ve been hearing my name called from the empty hallway at home, and that one time at the warehouse when nobody was in the aisle with me. I just can't get over it, because I cannot stress this enough, doctor—it sounds exactly as real as my husband standing right next to me. 

If it sounded like a ghost or a faint little whisper, maybe I could brush it off or blame it on the wind, but it's a solid, real voice. It has weight to it, if that makes sense. So, no, my eyes are fine, I'm not seeing visions, and I feel perfectly normal physically. It all just comes back to that voice. I keep trying to figure out if maybe the air conditioning vent in the hall is making a weird noise that just happens to sound exactly like my name, or if the metal racks at the warehouse were vibrating in some specific way, but... well, I know that sounds crazy when I say it out loud. It's just the voice. Nothing else.
Have you had any thoughts about why you might be hearing your name called, or if there's any special meaning behind it?

Well, honestly, that's the thing that's been driving me absolutely up the wall. I sit there on the couch, or I'll be driving to work, and my brain is just spinning like a hamster on a wheel trying to figure it out. Because you want there to be a reason, right? You want to think, 'Oh, it's my guardian angel,' or 'Oh, it's some kind of message from the universe,' or whatever it is people say on those daytime talk shows. But... no. I don't think it means anything special at all. 

I mean, I've tried to make sense of it. I really have. I sat down the other night with a cup of tea, after my husband went to bed, and I just stared at the wall thinking, 'Why my name? Why not a warning? Why not hello?' But there's no grand message. There's no feeling of, like, impending doom or some secret knowledge being passed down to me. It's just my name. It's like someone dialing a phone number, letting it ring once, and then hanging up. 

And that almost makes it worse, you know? Because if it was a message, at least I'd have something to work with. I could say, 'Okay, the voice wants me to buy a lottery ticket,' or whatever. But this? This is just senseless. It's just my brain—or my ears, or whatever is broken—just throwing my name out into the empty air for absolutely no reason. I keep thinking maybe it's stress from the warehouse, because they've been pushing us really hard on quotas lately, and my supervisor is always breathing down our necks. But then I think, why would stress make me hear my name in my own hallway when I'm just sorting socks? It doesn't add up. So, no, I don't think there's any special meaning. I just think something is wrong, and I just want it to stop.
Have you had any thoughts or beliefs that the voice you heard might be coming from a specific source, like someone watching you, a supernatural being, or a hidden device?

Oh, gosh, no. No, nothing like that. I mean, I watch those true crime shows on television where people find out their creepy landlord put a camera in the air vent or something, and sure, maybe that crosses your mind for half a second when you hear a voice out of nowhere, but... no. My husband and I own our house, we've lived there for fifteen years. Who on earth would be sneaking in to put a hidden speaker in our hallway? And for what? Just to say my name once in a blue moon and then turn it off? It doesn't make a lick of sense. I'm just a regular woman sorting boxes and fulfilling orders at a warehouse. I don't have government secrets, I don't have some crazy ex trying to stalk me, and I definitely don't have millions of dollars for anyone to steal. So the idea of someone watching me or setting up devices... no, that's just silly. 

And the supernatural stuff? Like ghosts or spirits? Look, my grandmother was very superstitious, she used to throw salt over her shoulder and wouldn't walk under ladders and all that, but I just don't buy into it. If my house was haunted, wouldn't a ghost do something a little more, I don't know, dramatic? Rattle some chains or knock over a lamp or at least say a full sentence? Just saying my first name sounds like a pretty boring haunting to me. 

So no, I don't think it's a ghost, or a demon, or the CIA, or anything crazy like that. Like I was trying to say before, I really just think it's my own ears playing tricks on me, or... or my brain misfiring somehow. It's just so incredibly frustrating because I'll literally look around the room, I'll peek behind the doors, I'll check if maybe the TV in the living room somehow turned itself on and connected to Bluetooth, but I know there's no one there. I know there's no hidden microphone. It's just me, and the quiet, and that voice. I keep going over it and over it, pacing around the house, trying to find a completely normal, boring explanation for it, but I absolutely do not think anyone is spying on me or haunting me. I just want my head to be quiet again.
Have you ever had any thoughts that others might not have, like believing something is true that most people would say is not, even if you couldn’t prove it?

Well, I don't know if this is exactly what you mean by believing something most people wouldn't, because it wasn't like... a conspiracy theory or anything crazy like that. But there was this whole thing a little while back with my crafts. 

See, I do these resin crafts—coasters and little jewelry trays with dried flowers and gold flakes pressed into them. I started doing it at the kitchen table because, honestly, standing on the concrete at the warehouse for ten hours a day just absolutely ruins your feet and your lower back, and I needed something pretty and quiet to focus on when I got home. But anyway, a few months ago, I just... I got it in my head that I could turn my crafts into a real retirement business right away. And I don't mean just selling a few at a local church bazaar or putting them on the internet for pocket change. I mean, I was absolutely convinced that this was going to be a massive empire that would replace my income, and my husband's income, like, overnight. 

I remember I had all my little silicone molds spread out all over the dining room, and I was drawing these elaborate charts in a spiral notebook, calculating how we'd be completely set for life by the end of the year. I was so sure of it. I thought everyone would see I had figured out the perfect plan for our family. I was practically vibrating with how brilliant I thought I was. My husband tried to bring me back down to earth—he was standing there in his pajamas, pointing out that I’d only ever sold two coasters to my cousin and that the resin takes a full twenty-four hours just to cure, so making ten thousand of them a week was physically impossible. 

But I wouldn't listen to a word he said. I just looked at him like he was the one who wasn't seeing reality. I literally believed I had unlocked some secret formula to wealth that nobody else was smart enough to see. I was ready to march into my supervisor's office at the warehouse the very next morning and quit on the spot because I just knew, without a shadow of a doubt, that my little kitchen table hobby was a million-dollar idea. I was even looking up commercial warehouse spaces to rent for my "headquarters." Looking back now, I know how unrealistic that sounds, but at the time, you couldn't have told me otherwise. I just felt so incredibly important and smart, like I was the only one who had our whole future perfectly figured out.

When you believed your crafts would become a million-dollar business overnight, did you feel that this idea was so powerful or special that it could only have come to you, or did it feel more like a realistic business plan that just needed hard work?

Well, you know, it definitely wasn't just about rolling up my sleeves and putting in the elbow grease. I mean, I work at a warehouse, I know exactly what hard work is! I know what it means to put in ten hours of physical labor, lifting and sorting until your feet are numb. So no, it wasn't like I thought, 'Oh, if I just work an extra forty hours a week making coasters, I'll slowly build up a little customer base over the next five years.' 

It was so much bigger than that. It felt... well, it felt like magic, honestly. I just got it in my head that I could turn my crafts into a real retirement business right away. Not eventually, but right that very second. I felt like I had this crystal clear vision, this incredibly powerful idea that was just sitting there in the universe waiting for someone smart enough to grab it, and I was that person. I honestly believed that I had unlocked the ultimate secret, and I kept thinking about how everyone would see I had figured out the perfect plan for our family. 

I wasn't thinking about the cost of epoxy resin or shipping delays or marketing strategies or any of that boring, realistic stuff you'd put in a normal business plan. I just kept picturing the look on my husband's face, and my sister's face, and even my supervisor at the warehouse—I kept imagining them all realizing how brilliant I was. I felt this overwhelming certainty that my idea was incredibly special, that I was special for thinking of it, and that it was going to catapult us into this entirely different life overnight. I was literally pacing the dining room floor, my heart was just racing because I was so excited about how flawless this plan was. I felt like an absolute genius, I really did. I just knew I was the only one who could have seen it so clearly, and I couldn't wait for everyone else to realize it too.

Have you ever had a time when you felt unusually high, extremely confident, or so full of energy that you didn’t feel like you needed much sleep, and you were doing things much more quickly or intensely than usual—like starting a lot of new projects or making big plans?

Oh, absolutely. That’s exactly what it was like during that whole resin craft thing I was just telling you about. I mean, at first I just felt so fired up, you know? I had this energy buzzing right under my skin, and I felt almost completely unstoppable about my craft business. I was staying up half the night pouring molds and drawing up my big plans, and I really didn't even care about sleep because I just had so much momentum. 

And it wasn't just the business, either. It kind of bled into everything else in my life. I started making all these new house rules, too, because suddenly I felt like everything we were doing was just too slow and inefficient. I completely reorganized the kitchen cabinets at, like, two in the morning, and I made this strict rule about how the mail had to be sorted the exact second it came through the door, and how the laundry had to be staged in the hallway. I had these rigid systems for everything all of a sudden because my brain was just going a mile a minute and I needed everything around me to keep up with my pace. 

But the hard part—and this is what makes me feel awful looking back on it—is that because I felt so unstoppable and I had all these massive plans, I had absolutely zero patience for anyone who wasn't on my exact wavelength. Especially my husband. Bless his heart, he's a very steady, patient man, but during that time, I would just snap at him over the absolute smallest comments. I mean, if he just asked a simple question about where the spatulas went after I rearranged the kitchen, or if he made one tiny little remark about how much space my molds were taking up on the dining table, I would just bite his head off. 

I would get so incredibly angry, so fast. It literally felt like he was intentionally trying to drag me down. I remember yelling at him, telling him he was trying to hold me back from my potential and ruin my business before it even started, just because he asked if I was ever coming to bed. I just felt this intense, irritable rush anytime he questioned my new house rules or my plans. It's embarrassing to think about now, how mean I was being, but at the time, I honestly felt like I was driving a racecar and he was throwing nails on the track. I just couldn't stand him—or anyone—being in my way.
During that time when you felt so full of energy and were making all these plans, did you feel your mood was unusually high or irritable for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least a week?

Oh, a week? Lord, it was definitely longer than a week. I mean, when you're in the middle of it, time just sort of stops making sense, doesn't it? Because I wasn't sleeping, like I said, so the days and nights just kind of melted into one long, continuous stretch of me pacing around the dining room and drawing up charts and snapping at my poor husband. But if I really sit down and look at the calendar, and think about when I first brought home that extra-large bulk order of epoxy resin and cleared off the table... yeah, it was way more than seven days. 

It was every single day, most of the day, just like you said. Honestly, this whole change from being so incredibly wound up and restless, to... well, to the point where I started actually hearing my name being called out loud when nobody else was even in the room—which is a whole other thing that just completely threw me for a loop—and then eventually just completely crashing... that whole thing has been going on for about three weeks. 

Three whole weeks of my life just turned completely upside down. And it didn't even stop when I went to work! I'd be at the warehouse, walking down those long concrete aisles with my scanner, and I'd just be so intensely agitated that the other order fillers were walking too slow. I'd be practically running with my cart, my heart just pounding, thinking about my grand plans, and then I'd get home and start the whole frantic routine all over again, organizing and yelling and planning. So, yes, to answer your question, it was definitely more than a week. It was three solid weeks of just... being on this runaway train before the crash finally hit me.
During that time when you felt so full of energy and were making all these plans, did you feel your mood was unusually high or irritable most of the day, nearly every day, for at least a week?

Well, like I was just saying a minute ago—and I know I can talk your ear off, so forgive me for repeating myself—but yes, it was definitely longer than a week. If I really sit down and map it out, this whole change... from being so incredibly wound up and restless, just constantly moving and planning and yelling about the kitchen cabinets, all the way to the point where I started actually hearing my name being called out when I was completely alone in a room... and then finally just crashing the way I did... that entire ordeal has been going on for about three weeks. 

Three full weeks. And I tell you, when you are in the thick of it, three weeks feels like three years. Because you don't get a break from it, you know? You don't just wake up one Tuesday and feel normal for a few hours. It was every single day, most of the day, just this constant, buzzing, irritable high, right up until my body and my brain just couldn't take it anymore and I crashed. So yes, doctor, to answer you again, it was absolutely more than seven days. It was a solid three weeks of my life just being completely turned upside down.

During that time when you felt so full of energy and were making all these plans, did you feel like you needed less sleep than usual, or were you able to go with much less sleep without feeling tired?

Oh, sleep was... honestly, sleep was practically non-existent. And the crazy thing is, I didn't even miss it! Normally, you know, working at the warehouse, if I don't get my solid seven or eight hours, my feet are just dragging on that concrete, my back aches, and I can barely look at my scanner by the end of my shift. 

But during those three weeks? It was completely different. For a while there, I was sleeping maybe two or three hours a night, tops. I'd finally lay down around 3:00 AM, mostly just because my husband would be practically begging me to come to bed and stop making noise in the kitchen, but then my eyes would just pop wide open at 5:00 or 5:30. And I wasn't groggy at all, not even a little bit. I was waking up completely ready to go. It was like somebody had plugged me directly into a wall socket! 

I'd just bounce right out from under the covers, completely bypass the coffee maker, and go straight out to the dining room to check on how my epoxy molds were curing from the night before. Laying in bed just felt like... well, it felt like a complete waste of time. Like every single minute I spent with my eyes closed was just wasting time that I desperately needed for my projects and my business plans. I had all these ideas for different color swirls and packaging, and I just couldn't understand why my husband or anyone else needed so much rest when I was running on two hours and getting so much done. I felt totally fine, physically, which is just so bizarre to think about now because if I tried to do that today, I'd be a complete zombie.

During that time when you felt so full of energy and were making all these plans, did you experience a period where your mood was so unusually high, expansive, or irritable that it was clearly different from your usual self, and this lasted for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least a week?

Well, yes, absolutely. I mean, it was night and day from how I usually am. Usually, I'm just, you know, going to work, coming home, making dinner, maybe watching a little TV... just a very regular, even-keeled kind of person. But during those three weeks? Oh, it was a completely different story. 

At first, I just felt so... fired up, you know? Just incredibly energized and almost unstoppable. I had all these massive plans for my epoxy resin craft business, and I was completely overhauling the house rules, deciding how everything needed to be organized and run. I felt like I finally had everything figured out, like I was operating on this higher level that nobody else could quite reach. 

But the flip side of that was... well, I was just so incredibly irritable. I mean, my poor husband, he couldn't say a single word without me just snapping his head off. If he made even the smallest comment, like asking if I was going to clean up the dining room table so we could eat, or suggesting I maybe take a break... I would just explode. I felt like he was deliberately trying to hold me back, you know? Like he was this anchor just dragging me down when I was trying to soar. I'd yell at him, I'd yell at the dog if he barked too loud, I'd just be so short-tempered and practically vibrating with frustration because everyone around me was just moving so slowly and not understanding my vision. It was definitely not my usual self, not by a long shot. It was just this intense, overwhelming feeling of being on top of the world but also being furious that nobody else was up there with me.

During that time when you felt so full of energy and were making all these plans, did you experience a distinct period where your mood was abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable that was clearly different from your usual mood and lasted for at least one week?

Well, like I was just telling you a second ago, doctor—and I don't mind repeating it, I know you have a checklist and you need to get all your notes right—but yes, absolutely. It was exactly like I was just saying. 

At first, I just felt so completely fired up. I mean, I felt almost unstoppable. I had all this energy pouring into my craft business, figuring out the epoxy curing times and the profit margins, and at the same time I was completely overhauling the house rules. I had this whole new system for how the kitchen needed to be organized and how the laundry should be sorted because my brain was just working so much faster and better than usual, and I could finally see how inefficient we had been living. I was just on top of the world with it. 

But then, just like I mentioned, the irritability would kick in, and I’d snap at my husband over the absolute smallest comment. He could just walk into the room and ask a simple question about dinner, or ask me to move my resin bottles off the good tablecloth, and I would just bite his head right off. I felt like he was deliberately trying to hold me back. It felt like I was on this bullet train, finally getting my life and my business together, and he was just throwing rocks at the wheels trying to slow me down. It was so frustrating! Because I was feeling so good, so... expansive, I guess is the word you used, but then he just couldn't keep up. And that made me so mad I could scream. So yes, to answer your question again, it was a very distinct change, it was definitely abnormally elevated and irritable, and it lasted way longer than a week. Like I said, it was three solid weeks of feeling exactly like that.

During that time when you felt so full of energy and were making all these plans, did you experience a period of at least one week where your mood was continuously abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable?

Okay, wait, I feel like we’re going in circles here, Doc. Are you testing my memory or is this a trick question? Because I swear we literally just went over this exact same thing! But, I mean, I'll say it again if you need me to, maybe I didn't explain it right the first two times. 

Yes, for that entire three weeks, it never stopped. Every single day. Like I was saying, at first I just felt so completely fired up. I was practically vibrating with all these ideas. I felt completely unstoppable, especially when it came to my craft business. I was telling you about the resin, right? Well, I had this whole massive vision for how we were going to make thousands of dollars selling these custom pieces, doing the weekend craft fairs, setting up an online store, the whole nine yards. And at the exact same time, I was completely tearing up the house rules. I mean, I was reorganizing everything. I color-coded the pantry, I redid the entire mudroom shoe situation, and I made this strict schedule for when the TV was allowed to be on because I realized we were all just wasting our potential. I was operating on a totally different frequency than everyone else in that house.

But then, because nobody else was on that frequency, I was just so irritable. Constant snapping. My husband would come into the kitchen—which was my workspace, obviously—and he’d make the absolute smallest comment. He’d ask something ridiculous like, "Honey, did you pay the water bill?" or "Can we maybe move these molds so I can sit down and eat?" And I would just completely lose my mind on him. I'd snap so hard. It wasn't just a little annoyance; it was this intense, boiling frustration because I felt like he was intentionally trying to drag me back down to his level. I felt like I was finally doing something important and he was just trying to hold me back because he didn't have the same drive I did. 

So yes, continuous, every day, for three weeks. Elevated, irritable, expansive... whatever words you have on your clipboard there, it was all of that. Do you need me to go into more detail about the house rules I set up, or did you get it all this time?

During that time when you felt so full of energy and were making all these plans, did you find yourself being much more active than usual—like doing a lot more tasks, starting new projects, or feeling restless and unable to sit still?

Oh, my goodness, yes. I mean, it was like I had this motor running inside me that just wouldn't shut off, no matter what time of day it was. You have to understand, my job is not easy. I work as an order filler down at the distribution warehouse, so I am on my feet on solid concrete for eight to ten hours a shift, lifting heavy boxes, walking miles up and down the aisles. Normally, when I clock out and get home, my feet are absolutely screaming and I just want to collapse into my recliner and not move a single muscle. 

But during those three weeks? Sleep and resting didn't even cross my mind. I was coming home from a full shift at the warehouse and I wouldn't even take my boots off before I started tearing through the closets. I literally pulled every single winter coat, every pair of shoes, every old board game out of the hall closet and piled it all in the living room because I decided the whole house needed a completely new organizational flow. And while I was doing that, I was rewriting all those schedules I told you about. Not just the TV rules, but meal prep schedules, laundry rotations, a whole new system. 

And then, right in the middle of all that physical stuff, my brain would just latch onto something else. I suddenly got completely obsessed with looking up genealogy records. I had my laptop balanced on a stack of plastic storage bins in the hallway while I was sorting through old scarves, and I was just frantically tracing my great-grandmother's lineage back to the 1800s, cross-referencing census data and ship manifests. I was making list after list after list—lists of supplies I needed for the resin business, lists of ancestors I needed to find death certificates for, lists of chores my husband was doing inefficiently. 

I literally couldn’t sit still. If I even tried to sit on the couch for two seconds, my skin felt like it was buzzing, like I was wasting precious time. My husband would beg me to just come watch a movie with him, and I'd be pacing back and forth behind the couch with a clipboard, reorganizing my lists, just vibrating with all this energy. There just weren't enough hours in the day for everything I needed to accomplish, so I just kept moving and moving and moving.

So, yes. Seven days, fourteen days, twenty-one days. Continuously. Yes. Please, please tell me you finally got that written down this time so we can talk about something else.

Oh, God. Yes. Yes, I did. It was... it was like hitting a brick wall at a hundred miles an hour. You know, for those three weeks, I was flying so high, doing so much, fighting with my husband because he couldn't keep up, and then... it just stopped. The engine just died. 

I remember it was a Tuesday. I woke up and I just... I couldn't move. I mean, physically, my body just felt like it was made of lead. All that buzzing energy, all that carbonation in my blood, it was just gone, completely drained out of me. And what replaced it was this... this incredible, suffocating heaviness. 

I didn't want to look at the resin supplies. I didn't care about the genealogy records. I didn't even care about the schedules I'd made. I just... I dragged myself out of bed, and I made it as far as the kitchen table, and I just sat there. And I started crying. And I wasn't even crying about anything specific, you know? It wasn't like I was sad about a movie or a memory or an argument. It was just this deep, empty, hollow feeling, like someone had scooped out all my insides.
